summary:
Solomon Islands criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women under Penal Code provisions inherited from the colonial period, with a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. The ILGA World Database entry and the Human Dignity Trust country profile both record the offence, the historic-law basis and the same statutory maximum; a general reference summary repeats the figure of up to 14 years.

Enforcement is absent from the record. The United States State Department's annual human-rights reports for 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 record no arrests or prosecutions directed at LGBT people, the 2011 report records no LGBT-specific abuses, and the 2013 report records no abuses by security forces while noting the penal code provisions and no prosecutions under them. Human Dignity Trust documents no recorded prosecutions in recent years, and reference coverage states plainly that the law is not enforced. A visitor's exposure therefore rests on the statute remaining in force and on social and official responses, not on an active prosecution campaign.

Successive governments have refused reform. The Law Reform Commission proposed legalising gay and lesbian sexual activity in December 2008, and the proposal was strongly opposed. The government told the United Nations in 2011 that it had no intention of decriminalising homosexuality. Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare publicly opposed same-sex marriage in a 2017 speech to a local church group, and in June 2018 Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used his Queen's Birthday address to warn that same-sex marriage cannot populate the world, while also acknowledging in the same period that being gay or lesbian is said to be biological and beyond individual control yet citing both the criminal code and the Bible against any legal change.

No protective framework accompanies the offence. Same-sex couples have no relationship recognition, there is no non-discrimination shield covering sexual orientation, and no same-sex marriage law exists; Parliament has not legislated one. Constitutional reform has narrowed visibility of the issue: a 2009 draft constitution listed sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination, but the 2011, 2013 and 2014 drafts dropped it, with reform still ongoing as of 2019.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility is rhetorical rather than prosecutorial. The strongest statements in the record come from the head of government and the head of state addressing church and national audiences, which points to a social and reputational risk for an openly visible trans visitor rather than a realistic prospect of criminal proceedings. No source in the inventory records an arrest, charge or conviction for same-sex conduct at any point in the periods covered.

The reform trajectory runs against the visitor's interest. A formal decriminalisation proposal from the Law Reform Commission in 2008 was met with strong opposition, the government ruled out decriminalisation in a United Nations communication in 2011, and the equality language present in the 2009 constitutional draft was removed from every subsequent draft. A visitor assessing prospects should treat the current legal position as stable rather than transitional.

The wider human-rights reporting in the State Department material covers matters that do not bear directly on trans visitors, including pretrial detention, corruption and violence against women; these are general country conditions rather than identity-specific risks.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same 14-year maximum as visitors, but the record shows no enforcement against anyone for consensual same-sex conduct across the 2010 to 2013 reporting years, and no prosecutions in recent years according to Human Dignity Trust. The practical position for residents is an unenforced statute combined with the absence of any statutory protection.

Residents have no constitutional or statutory recourse on sexual-orientation grounds. The 2009 draft constitution would have prohibited discrimination on sexual orientation, but the 2011, 2013 and 2014 drafts dropped the ground and constitutional reform remained ongoing as of 2019, leaving no non-discrimination shield and no relationship recognition in force.

Domestic advocacy has been attempted and rebuffed. The Law Reform Commission's December 2008 recommendation to legalise gay and lesbian sexual activity was strongly opposed, and the government's stated position to the United Nations in 2011 was that it did not intend to decriminalise. Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare's 2017 church-group speech and Governor General Sir Frank Kabui's June 2018 Queen's Birthday address set out the official line against same-sex marriage and against changing the law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement data in the inventory stops at the 2013 reporting year. No source here covers arrests, police conduct or prosecutions after 2013, so the current enforcement position is unresolved rather than confirmed as unchanged.

The inventory contains nothing on gender identity specifically: no source addresses legal recognition of gender, identity-document or passport marker rules, screening at ports of entry, or the treatment of trans travellers as distinct from lesbians, gay men and bisexual people. Any trans-specific finding would be unsourced.

Also not sourced: hate-crime or bias-motivation provisions, hate-speech law, access to gender-affirming healthcare, prostitution or public-order offences that could be used against trans people, and rules on entry and visa refusal. The constitutional reform process is described only as ongoing as of 2019, with no later status in the record.
